Rhythm Library

Named timelines and cycles to hear and play along with: son and rumba clave (3-2, 2-3, 12/8), Toussaint’s six 4/4 and ten 12/8 bell patterns, tresillo, habanera, cinquillo, baqueteo, and their rotations, each from a cited source.

A timeline is a short pattern, often on a bell or claves, that repeats through a whole piece and keeps the band together. Further down are the metric cycles of India (Hindustani tāl, Carnatic tāḷa) and of Chinese opera, which are kept by hand gestures and drum strokes rather than one bell part. Every grid below comes from a source (named on its card): x is a stroke, . a silent pulse. Gaps counts the pulses from each stroke to the next. Each card plays the pattern (wood) over the main beats (kick); click a layer’s name to mute it and clap it yourself.

The six 4/4 timelines (Toussaint)

Godfried Toussaint (2002) compared six five-stroke timelines in sixteen pulses. Three come from Africa (Shiko, Soukous, Gahu) and three from the Americas (son, rumba, bossa nova); each differs from son clave by moving one or two strokes a pulse.

Claves: 2-3, 3-2 and 12/8 forms

Tresillo and its family

Eight pulses: one bar of 2/4 in sixteenths (or 4/4 in eighths).

The ten 12/8 bell patterns (Toussaint)

Toussaint (2003) collected ten seven-stroke bell patterns in twelve pulses; all are rearrangements of five gaps of 2 and two of 1.

Shiko rotations and Arabic drum timelines

The same five strokes started from a different note give a different named rhythm.

Brazilian bells and surdo

Two bars of 2/4 in sixteenths, copied from the list in Wikipedia’s “Clave (rhythm)” article (L low bell, H high bell, O open surdo, X muffled surdo; each sound is its own layer in the player). The article gives no source for the list, so treat it as one transcription among several. “3:2” and “2:3” say which bar has three strokes, as with Cuban clave.

Hindustani tāl (North India)

A tāl is a cycle of a fixed number of mātrās (beats), split into vibhāgs (sections); one cycle is an āvartan (Kippen 112; Clayton 43). The first mātrā is the sam (marked X). Each vibhāg starts with a hand gesture: a clap (tālī, numbered 2, 3 …) or a wave (khālī, “empty”, marked 0) (Kippen 112). On tabla or pakhavaj the cycle is played as a theka, a fixed pattern of strokes (bols); for Kippen the pattern, not the clapping, “is the primary description of a tala” (111), and for Clayton a tāl is the two together (60). Thekas vary between players and with tempo (Kippen 116).

Things the textbooks simplify:

  • Khālī is not simply “unaccented”: Kippen finds “far too many examples” against that (112). The rule that khālī bols drop the bass stroke (dhin becomes tin) holds for jhaptāl and rūpak; in tīntāl the tin tin sounds a mātrā late, and the rule is “a relatively recent development” (Clayton 62-66).
  • There is no fixed tempo (lay). Clayton measured vocal performances from about 10 mātrās a minute (slow vilambit) to 500 (fast drut); below about 30 a minute clapping stops working and listeners follow the theka (62, 84-86).
  • A tihāī is a phrase played three times to end on sam (Kippen 129; Clayton 168).

Thekas below are Kippen’s (Garland, 2000), checked against Clayton’s table (Ex. 5.1) and Courtney; each card notes where they differ. The player gives the claps, the waves and every mātrā: mute the claps and keep them yourself.

Carnatic tāḷa (South India)

A Carnatic tāḷa is built from three parts (aṅgas), each shown with the hand (kriyas; Nelson 139-40):

  • Anudrutam (U): one beat, “a solitary clap”.
  • Drutam (O): two beats, “a clap followed by a wave of the hand” (palm turned up).
  • Laghu (l): “a clap followed by counts on the fingers”, from the pinkie (pinkie, ring, middle, index, thumb, then the pinkie again for 7 and 9). Its length is its jāti: tisra 3, chatusra 4, khanda 5, misra 7, sankirna 9.

Seven families (the suladi tāḷas) times five jātis give 35 tāḷas, from 3 beats (tisra Eka) to 29 (sankirna Dhruva). Each beat is then split into a gati (nadai): 4 pulses by default (ta ka di mi), or 3, 5, 7 or 9. Nelson: of the 35 “only five are in common use”: khanda Aṭa (14), misra Jhampa (10), chatusra Triputa = Ādi (8), Rūpaka (6, almost always counted as 3) and tisra Eka (3) (141). The chāpu tāḷas sit outside the scheme. Tempo stays steady while the music gets denser, unlike Hindustani music, which speeds up (148). A mora is a phrase stated three times with gaps, ending on a set point, like the tihāī; a korvai is a longer composition ending in a mora; eḍuppu is where the song starts in the cycle, often on or just after the first beat (146, 155-56).

Tāḷa Aṅgas Tisra (3) Chatusra (4) Khanda (5) Misra (7) Sankeerna (9)
Dhruva l O l l 11 14 17 23 29
Matya l O l 8 10 12 16 20
Rupaka O l 5 6 7 9 11
Jhampa l U O 6 7 8 10 12
Triputa l O O 7 8 9 11 13
Ata l l O O 10 12 14 18 22
Eka l 3 4 5 7 9

Chinese opera: ban and yan

In jingju (Beijing opera), “every metered metrical type provides a pattern of accented beats (ban) and unaccented beats (yan, lit. ‘eyes’)” (Wichmann 59). The conductor plays both the wooden clapper (ban) and the small clapper-drum (bangu): the clapper is struck “firmly on every accented beat”; on unaccented beats the conductor may strike the drum with one stick, or touch the clapper lightly (238). Gongche notation writes the two as marks beside the notes (。 ban, 、 yan) without note lengths.

Each section of an aria is set in a banshi (“accented-beat style”). Wichmann counts six metered types, three free ones, and huilong, which only follows daoban (59-70); most have an xipi and an erhuang version (70). Her Fig. 7 (66) writes the metered ones as X (ban) and O (yan):

Banshi Pattern Metre Tempo and feel (Wichmann)
慢板 manban, slow X O O O 4/4 Slowest; “relatively peaceful, introspective situations” (61)
快三眼 kuaisanyan, fast three eyes X O O O 4/4 About twice as fast as manban; introspective or plain narration (62-63)
原板 yuanban, primary X O X O 2/4 About 72 beats a minute, “like a healthy resting heart”; narration, facts, explanation (59-61)
二六 erliu, two-six X O X O 2/4 (fast two-six 1/4) Faster than yuanban; “a sense of excitement or anticipation” (64-65)
流水 liushui, flowing water X X X X 1/4 Excitement approaching that of kuaiban (64-65)
快板 kuaiban, fast X X X X 1/4 Fastest; “highly animated”, excitement or anticipation (62)
散板 sanban, dispersed free none Moderate; “less tense, more gentle” (67)
导板 daoban, lead free none From slower than manban up; often one line; “sudden grief, extreme unhappy surprise” (68-69)
回龙 huilong, undulating dragon after daoban takes the next type’s Metered (68)
摇板 yaoban free singing 1/4 band Sung freely over liushui’s single-beat percussion: “exterior calm and interior tension” (69-70)

In xipi the first syllable of a line starts on a yan and the last on a ban; in erhuang both start on a ban (72-73).

The percussion, “the four major pieces”, is drum and clapper, large gong, small gong and cymbals (233, 239), playing more than a hundred named passages (luogu dian, “gong and drum points”). Players say each stroke as a syllable (240): kuang large gong; cang large gong with small gong and cymbals; tai (dei) small gong; qi (qie) cymbals; da drum, right stick; zha clapper, firm; yi clapper, light. Wichmann prints the passages in her own letter notation; one scene opener, Charging Head (Chong tou), is da, a drum roll, then cang cei repeated, ending cang cei cang (261).

Not here yet

  • African 4/4 bells, Afro-Brazilian bells (Wikipedia “Bell pattern”), kadodo, afrekete and Abakuá bells: shown there only as staff images, with no grid or counts in the text.
  • Songo and cáscara: Wikipedia shows them only as images; its sources are Peñalosa, Rumba Quinto (2010, pp. 141-44), and Changuito, A Master’s Approach to Timbales (1998), not read for this page.
  • Second line: Wikipedia’s article prints no rhythm and cites nothing for its drumming.
  • Samba (full batucada), partido alto as a guitar / pandeiro pattern: only the bell lines above have a written grid.
  • Chinese percussion passages as players: Wichmann prints them in her own letter notation, not yet turned into players.
  • Partido alto, cáscara, songo, second line, kadodo, afrekete, Abakuá: not in Toussaint’s book either; Peñalosa’s books are the next place to look.
